## Deep Dive

<doc title="gRPC services" path="./docs/internal/grpc-services/">
# gRPC services

Five internal gRPC services expose domain operations over mTLS-protected connections.

## Users service

Registration, login, user lookup, and preference updates.

## Workflows service

Workflow CRUD, build status, list filters, failure counters, termination, deletion, and internal lookup by ID.

## Jobs service

Scheduling, reads, status updates, lease claim and renewal, container attachment, completion, failure, cancellation, retry release, expired-lease recovery, logs, search, live streaming, and job listing.

`FailJob` requires a failure-family terminal reason code, while `CancelJob` and `CancelClaimedJob` require a cancellation-family code. Workers must use the dedicated terminal commands so failure kind, diagnostics, status, reason, and replay identity are recorded together. Job list and public detail responses expose only the normalized safe code and message, never the stored raw error.

### Container cleanup RPCs

These are admin-authorized internal gRPC operations, not routes in the public
HTTP OpenAPI document. They use the messages in `proto/jobs/jobs.proto`.
Every request identifies `job_id` and `intent_id` as UUIDs, the immutable
`container_id`, and the original `runtime_instance`. Clients invoke named RPCs;
the uppercase operation constants are internal dispatch values, not request fields.

| RPC | Additional request / result contract |
| --- | --- |
| `GetContainerCleanupReceipt` | Returns whether that exact identity has recorded completion proof |
| `RecordContainerCleanupReceipt` | Records caller-verified original-instance removal/absence and releases only the corresponding hold |
| `BeginContainerCleanupAttempt` | Requires a positive expected cleanup `generation`; `PROCESSING` with a token grants one attempt |
| `FailContainerCleanupAttempt` | Requires the generation, Begin token and a nonempty, non-OK `error_code` of up to 32 bytes; `interrupted` reports caller cancellation |
| `RedriveContainerCleanup` | Requires the generation and a nonblank `reason` of at most 2048 bytes; an accepted transition is audited with the validated JWT subject |

Cleanup generations are independent of workflow generations. Attempt responses
contain `state`, `generation`, `attempts` and `token`; audit identity/reason/time is
persisted separately, not added to public job responses. A stale redrive returns
`STALE` and a completed identity returns `COMPLETED`, without another requeue.
A live cleanup lease prevents redrive.

Receipt callers must confirm removal or absence on the verified original daemon
before recording proof. Jobs-service validates stored materialization provenance
and commits receipt/hold changes; it does not perform the Docker removal itself.

The service rejects redrive without an authenticated admin subject. An actor is
never accepted from request fields or unvalidated metadata. Audit actor values
are limited to 256 bytes. Shared service credentials cannot provide individual
human attribution.

Jobs-service also owns creation-intent Ensure/observation/Create/Start reservation,
discovery claim/report and admin inspection/redrive RPCs. Single-use mutation grants
are not replayed. `RedriveContainerIntent` controls discovery inspection and has
separate generation/audit state from cleanup execution.

[Recovery examples and audit inspection](./docs/operations/recovery#container-cleanup)

<SourceLink path="proto/jobs/jobs.proto">Jobs protobuf messages and RPC definitions</SourceLink>

## Notifications service

Notification creation, listing, and marking records read.

## Analytics service

User and workflow aggregate reads.

## Transport security

Compose configures service certificates, client certificates, CA trust, and signed authorization metadata. Direct host exposure of development ports is for debugging, not a substitute for authenticated service calls.

In Kubernetes, these five services use headless Service discovery. DNS returns
ready Pod IPs to the gRPC clients, whose `round_robin` policy distributes calls
across the resolved replicas instead of multiplexing every call through one
ClusterIP connection.
</doc>

<doc title="Kafka events" path="./docs/internal/kafka-events/">
# Kafka events

Kafka events connect the durable state owned by services with the asynchronous work owned by workers.

## Topic contracts

- `workflows`: build, reschedule, termination, deletion, workflow terminal effects, and immutable container-cleanup snapshots.
- `jobs`: dispatch and container execution work.
- `job_logs`: deterministic retained stdout and stderr events.
- `analytics`: workflow, job, and log aggregate inputs.

## Event identity

Events carry stable identifiers or deterministic keys for replay-sensitive side effects. Workflow generation and job dispatch attempt fields provide additional stale-work protection.

A container-cleanup event carries the job/full container ID, original runtime
routing/instance and intent identity. Its cleanup generation is independent of
workflow generation. Duplicate delivery does not create another execution budget
or inflate cleanup backlog gauges. Administrative redrive advances the retained
cleanup generation, leaving older reports/deliveries stale.

## Trace headers

OpenTelemetry propagation fields are injected into Kafka headers and extracted by consumers.

## Compatibility

Event schema changes must account for records already present in Kafka. Additive changes are preferred, and consumers must not assume a producer and every consumer deploy simultaneously.

## Delivery expectation

Events are delivered at least once. Consumers must remain idempotent, preconditioned, or deduplicated.
</doc>

<doc title="Data stores" path="./docs/internal/data-stores/">
# Data stores

## PostgreSQL

Stores users, workflows, jobs, runtime nodes, notification state, analytics aggregates, idempotency records, outbox rows, job leases, retry metadata, and processed-event identity.

### Container lifecycle records

Jobs-service owns the durable container protocol in PostgreSQL:

| Record | Authority / retention |
| --- | --- |
| `container_creation_intents` | Per-attempt name, original routing/instance, single-use grants and monotonic closure; retained for late discovery |
| `container_materializations` | Verified immutable IDs; one daemon/container identity cannot belong to multiple intents |
| `runtime_capacity_holds` | Unresolved Start-reserved physical capacity; released only by matching removal proof |
| `container_cleanup_receipts` | Exact original-instance completion evidence; repeated acknowledgment cannot release capacity twice |
| `outbox_events` cleanup fields | Execution generation, token/lease, retry budget, backoff and quarantine on the retained cleanup intent |
| `container_cleanup_redrives` | Accepted cleanup generation changes with authenticated actor, repair reason and timestamp; survives source/outbox pruning |
| `container_intent_redrives` | Separate audit of administrative discovery-inspection redrive |

Durable-state gauges read unfinished cleanup rather than counting deliveries.
Audit retention is separate from outbox retention. Neither elapsed age nor an
audit record replaces physical removal proof.

## ClickHouse

Stores retained job logs optimized for high-volume ordered reads. It is not the authoritative workflow or job state store.

## Redis

Stores HTTP sessions, cached service reads, live log pub/sub state, and runtime-node-scoped image-pull locks.

## Meilisearch

Indexes retained log messages for text search and highlights. ClickHouse remains the retained log body store.

## Kafka

Carries durable asynchronous events. It is a transport log, not the only record of command completion or job ownership.

## Runtime registry and Docker proxy

`runtime-agent` registers Docker-capable nodes in PostgreSQL and heartbeats Docker endpoint health, capacity, and status. The Docker proxy exposes a token-authenticated, method-and-path-allowlisted subset of Docker APIs to workers instead of mounting the daemon socket directly into every process.

`runtime-agent` owns rows in `runtime_nodes`. Jobs store `runtime_node_id` and an endpoint snapshot while they are running so execution, logs, termination, deletion, and expired-lease recovery use the Docker daemon that owns the container.

## Ownership rule

Do not add a second writable source for a domain entity without defining reconciliation. Each store has a distinct operational role.
</doc>

<doc title="Monitoring" path="./docs/operations/monitoring/">
# Monitoring

## Compose health

Start with `docker compose ps` and identify the first unhealthy dependency. Application failures often originate in certificate generation, infrastructure readiness, topic initialization, or migrations.

## Health checks

Compose checks PostgreSQL with TLS `psql`, ClickHouse with the secure client, Redis with TLS, Meilisearch over HTTPS, and gRPC services with authenticated TLS probes.

## Service signals

Monitor request and RPC latency, Kafka consumer progress, outbox pending and dead rows, expired job leases, execution retries, log processor batch failures, ClickHouse insert latency, Meilisearch health, and database pool saturation.

For endpoint traffic, use histogram counts for request rate, status-code attributes for error ratios, and histogram buckets for latency percentiles. Group REST traffic by `http.route` rather than raw URL paths, and group gRPC traffic by `rpc.service` and `rpc.method`.

## Container cleanup signals

Use the [durable cleanup gauges](./docs/operations/observability#durable-cleanup-metrics)
to distinguish execution failures from publication failures:

| Signal | First response |
| --- | --- |
| Sustained nonzero `quarantined` | Inspect the retained failure and original runtime, repair it, then request an audited redrive |
| Sustained nonzero `publication_dead` | Inspect outbox/Kafka publication before redriving the retained cleanup |
| Rising `oldest_due` | Check consumer progress, abandoned execution leases, connectivity and repeated worker interruptions |
| Rising `outstanding` | Compare arrival and completion rates; backlog alone does not prove failure |

Use max across jobs-service replicas because each reports the same durable state.
Choose age thresholds above normal delivery latency; five minutes overdue sustained
for five minutes is an initial example to tune for the deployment. This threshold
measures waiting execution, independently of the publisher's replay interval. A
future replay deadline does not mean cleanup must wait: existing Kafka deliveries
can still run. If no usable delivery remains, execution may depend on the next
eligible replay. Cross-check `cleanup_replay_due_at`, publication state and
consumer progress before diagnosing a stuck worker; `publication_dead` still
requires operator repair. Missing telemetry is not a zero backlog.

Quarantine does not prove removal and does not release a workflow admission gate
or runtime capacity hold. Use the [cleanup recovery procedure](./docs/operations/recovery#container-cleanup)
and the retained-row queries in the runbook to identify affected work.

<SourceLink path="docs/operations.md">Cleanup inspection SQL and operational thresholds</SourceLink>

## User-visible checks

Track scheduling delay, workflow build failures, jobs stuck outside terminal states, SSE connection failures, missing retained logs, and analytics lag.

## First response

```bash
docker compose -f compose.prod.yaml ps
docker compose -f compose.prod.yaml logs --since=15m server
docker compose -f compose.prod.yaml logs --since=15m outbox-relay
docker compose -f compose.prod.yaml logs --since=15m execution-worker
```
</doc>

<doc title="Observability" path="./docs/operations/observability/">
# Observability

Chronoverse emits OpenTelemetry traces, metrics, and structured logs to the bundled Grafana OTEL LGTM stack.

## Collection

Services and workers export over OTLP gRPC to `lgtm:4317`. The Grafana UI is
available inside the `lgtm` container on port `3000`, but is not host-published
by default. Anonymous access is disabled (`GF_AUTH_ANONYMOUS_ENABLED=false`);
authenticate with `GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_USER` / `GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_PASSWORD`.

## Grafana access

For Kubernetes, use
`kubectl -n chronoverse port-forward svc/lgtm 3000:3000`. For Compose, use the
opt-in loopback override:

```sh
docker compose -f compose.dev.yaml -f compose.grafana.yaml up -d lgtm
```

`compose.grafana.yaml` publishes
`127.0.0.1:${GRAFANA_HOST_PORT:-3000}:3000`; it does not expose Grafana to the
LAN.

To rotate the Compose administrator password, update
`GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_PASSWORD`, recreate `lgtm` with the same administrator
username, and apply the password to Grafana's database:

```sh
docker compose -f compose.dev.yaml up -d --force-recreate --no-deps lgtm
scripts/grafana/reset-admin-password.sh
```

The helper uses Grafana CLI, passes the password through standard input, and
verifies anonymous requests return `401` and configured credentials return
`200`. Preserve `lgtm:/data`: it contains the Grafana database and dashboards,
Prometheus metrics, Loki logs, Tempo traces, and Pyroscope profiles.

## Built-in dashboard

Every environment file-provisions a `chronoverse` Grafana dashboard from
`infra/k8s/base/grafana-dashboards/chronoverse.json` (Compose bind-mounts the
directory; Kubernetes serves it from hashed ConfigMaps that Grafana re-polls
every 30 seconds). It covers HTTP/gRPC request rates, p95 latency, latency
heatmaps, 5xx ratios, Go runtime (goroutines, memory, CPU), log volume and
error logs, and a fleet table, with links into Explore for traces and logs.
The LGTM image's bundled demo dashboards are disabled by an empty provider
(`defaults-off.yaml`) because provisioned dashboards cannot be removed through
the Grafana UI.

## Traces

Trace context crosses HTTP, gRPC, and Kafka. Use a single trace to follow an API mutation into outbox publication, worker processing, domain RPCs, and follow-up events.

## Metrics

Runtime and host metrics complement application spans. HTTP, gRPC, and Redis instrumentation uses the same global OpenTelemetry meter provider and exports through the configured OTLP endpoint.

### Endpoint metrics

The HTTP server emits the standard OpenTelemetry histograms:

- `http.server.request.duration`
- `http.server.request.body.size`
- `http.server.response.body.size`

Outbound heartbeat requests emit the corresponding `http.client.*` metrics. HTTP server metrics use route templates such as `/workflows/{workflow_id}`; workflow IDs, job IDs, users, URLs, and authentication data are not metric attributes.

All gRPC servers and clients emit:

- `rpc.server.call.duration` and `rpc.client.call.duration`
- per-RPC request and response message counts

Useful dimensions include HTTP method, route, and response status, plus gRPC service, method, and status code. Unary and streaming RPCs are both recorded.

Request volume is derived from histogram sample counts rather than a separate request counter. In Grafana's Prometheus data source, the OTEL metrics are normalized to Prometheus names. Example queries include:

```promql
# REST requests per second by route and method
sum by (http_route, http_request_method) (
  rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count[5m])
)

# REST 5xx ratio
sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{http_response_status_code=~"5.."}[5m]))
/
sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count[5m]))

# REST p95 latency by route
histogram_quantile(
  0.95,
  sum by (le, http_route) (rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))
)

# gRPC requests per second by service and method
sum by (rpc_service, rpc_method) (
  rate(rpc_server_call_duration_seconds_count[5m])
)
```

Watch latency distributions, error ratios, and saturation rather than relying only on process uptime.

### Durable cleanup metrics

Jobs-service exports cleanup backlog gauges from committed PostgreSQL state:

| OTLP metric | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `chronoverse.container_cleanup.outstanding` | All unfinished container cleanup, including quarantined work and dead publication |
| `chronoverse.container_cleanup.quarantined` | Execution quarantines requiring operator repair and redrive |
| `chronoverse.container_cleanup.publication_dead` | Unfinished cleanup whose outbox publication is `DEAD` |
| `chronoverse.container_cleanup.oldest_due` | Seconds overdue for cleanup execution, excluding active cleanup leases, future execution backoff and quarantined work |

`oldest_due` follows execution eligibility, not the next republication deadline.
A delivery already in Kafka can execute while its next replay is scheduled for
later. Replay pacing does not pause or reset this age; execution leases and
execution retry backoff do. This keeps stalled cleanup visible during a long
replay interval. If no usable delivery remains in Kafka, execution may depend on
the next eligible replay. Check its due time, publication state and consumer
progress alongside this gauge when diagnosing overdue cleanup.

These are gauges of retained work, not counts of deliveries or log lines.
Duplicate delivery and exporter restarts do not increase the backlog. A matching
completion receipt removes the cleanup from every measurement. No job, container,
runtime or actor identity is exported as a metric label.

Every jobs-service replica reads the same database totals. Aggregate replicas
with **max**, not sum. Collection has a five-second deadline and honors an earlier
caller deadline. A failed collection omits samples rather than reporting a healthy
zero; monitor telemetry availability separately.

See [monitoring](./docs/operations/monitoring) for alert interpretation and
[recovery](./docs/operations/recovery) for diagnosis, redrive and audit history.
These signals are available through the existing telemetry pipeline; the built-in
request/runtime dashboard does not provision cleanup-specific panels or alerts.

<SourceLink path="internal/repository/jobs/cleanup_metrics.go">Cleanup metric definitions and collection</SourceLink>

### Durable discovery metrics

Jobs-service exports discovery backlog gauges from committed intent state:

| OTLP metric | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `chronoverse.container_intents.discovery_due{lane}` | Closed, non-quarantined intents scheduled due, split by `URGENT` and `SURVEILLANCE` |
| `chronoverse.container_intents.oldest_due{lane}` | Seconds since the oldest scheduled due time in that lane, including due rows that still hold an inspection lease |
| `chronoverse.container_intents.quarantined` | Quarantined intents requiring repair before redrive |
| `chronoverse.container_intents.capacity_holds` | Unreleased Start-reserved capacity holds |

A successful read always reports both lanes, with an explicit zero for an empty
lane, and never an unlabeled total beside them. Lane is the only attribute; no
job, intent or runtime identity is exported. Scheduled-due age is not claimable
waiting age because a due row can still hold its 45-second inspection lease, so
inspect active leases separately and compare the maximum lane age.

The marker is a conservative scheduling hint, not proof, admission or mutation
authority. First closure starts in the urgent lane at closure time, a duplicate
closure preserves the marker and due time, a new unreceipted materialization
promotes, and only a successful fenced report may downgrade when no active hold or
unreceipted materialization remains. Errors, quarantine, redrive and authority
rules are unchanged. Claims lock a durable turn, split the batch between the
preferred lane and the other, borrow unused capacity, then interleave the final
response starting with the preferred lane when nonempty; the turn advances
opposite that first served lane in the same transaction as the tokens. Batch
sizes, rearm, lease, backoff and pass timing are unchanged, and no new setting is
introduced.

Claim selection uses the lane/due index and materializes candidate IDs before
updating leases. Healthy reports use full-key receipt probes for the current
intent. Recheck both query plans after PostgreSQL or predicate/index changes,
including generic plans and intents with many materializations; indexed selection
alone does not guarantee an efficient update or receipt join.

Every jobs-service replica reads the same database totals; aggregate with **max**,
not sum. Failed collection omits samples rather than reporting a healthy zero.

<SourceLink path="internal/repository/jobs/container_intent_metrics.go">Discovery lane metric definitions and collection</SourceLink>

## Logs

Structured application logs include service context and trace correlation where available. Container job stdout and stderr are a separate product data stream and follow the live/retained log pipeline.

## Investigation order

Start from the user-visible request or job ID, locate its trace, inspect failed spans and correlated logs, then confirm durable state in PostgreSQL and transport progress in Kafka.
</doc>

<doc title="Scaling" path="./docs/operations/scaling/">
# Scaling

## Kafka partitions

Consumer throughput is bounded by partition count. Production defaults use more partitions for `jobs` and `job_logs` than for lower-volume workflow and analytics traffic.

## Execution workers

Scale concurrency only when registered runtime capacity, Docker CPU, memory, image bandwidth, Kafka partitions, jobs-service latency, and lease-renewal headroom support it.

Execution worker container limits protect the worker process. `EXECUTION_WORKER_WORKLOAD_CONTAINER_*` limits protect each Docker workload container launched by the worker, and do not apply to image pulls. `EXECUTION_WORKER_WORKLOAD_NETWORK` names the dedicated Docker network every workload attaches to (default `chronoverse-workloads`, created on demand with inter-container communication disabled). Custom names must match `[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9_.-]*`; the runtime revalidates the network before every container creation and recreates it after a safe prune. The network is pinned to `EXECUTION_WORKER_WORKLOAD_SUBNET` (default `198.18.247.0/24`) with host-firewall egress filtering; see Certificates and security.

Execution workers do not need to run on the same node as the Docker daemon. They receive `runtime_endpoint` from `jobs-service` and use the direct Docker data plane for image ensure, container start, logs, and cleanup.

## Runtime agents

Run one runtime agent beside each Docker-capable daemon. New container claims only use fresh `READY` runtime rows. Missing heartbeats pause new claims for that runtime, while expired-lease recovery uses the stored job owner to decide whether to clean up or retry.

Kubernetes runtime endpoints are node IPs on mTLS `:2376` via `hostNetwork`, not a load-balanced Service. Every labeled node must expose Docker Engine and be routable from every worker. Client caches are bounded to 256 endpoints with 30-minute idle and LRU eviction, so node churn does not grow worker memory without limit. containerd-only clusters are not Docker-workflow runtimes; multi-node kind-like emulators require an explicit cross-node reachability test.

Role certificates scale with replicas: workflow-worker replicas share the workflow role and execution-worker replicas share the execution role, while each role is mounted separately. This separates privilege classes, not individual pod identities. A compromised execution role remains node-root-equivalent because it can create containers; use isolated/rootless runtime pools when that shared role blast radius is unacceptable.

## Workflow workers

Replicas that share a runtime node coordinate identical image pulls through Redis. Different runtime nodes still pull independently. Docker host is used as a fallback when runtime scope is omitted. Build completion records the resolved workflow image digest; execution workers ensure that digest on the assigned runtime node before creating the container.

## Outbox relay

Multiple replicas use processing leases. Tune batch size and polling against PostgreSQL and Kafka latency, not in isolation.

## Logs

High log volume requires sufficient `job_logs` partitions, processor replicas, ClickHouse insertion capacity, Meilisearch indexing capacity, and network throughput.

## Databases

Review every service's connection pool when increasing replicas. Replica multiplication can exhaust PostgreSQL, ClickHouse, Redis, or Meilisearch before CPU becomes the limiting resource.

### Retained cleanup data

Cleanup receipts, creation intents and materializations survive source deletion
and transport pruning. Retained proof and unfinished work can therefore grow even
when the queue is quiet. Use the following on-demand reports to inspect that
storage and decide whether to investigate cleanup or expand deployment capacity.

Save the SQL blocks below as `retention-inventory.sql` and `retention-backlog.sql`.
Use an observer libpq service profile with database CONNECT, public-schema USAGE
and SELECT on the seven reported tables; superuser privileges are not required.
Keep credentials out of command-line URIs and captured samples.

```sh
PGCONNECT_TIMEOUT=5 psql -X -qAt -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 \
  'service=chronoverse-observer' -f retention-inventory.sql
PGCONNECT_TIMEOUT=5 psql -X -qAt -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 \
  'service=chronoverse-observer' -f retention-backlog.sql
```

Both reports use read-only transactions, UTC and a one-second lock timeout. The
inventory SELECT has a five-second statement deadline and the exact backlog
SELECT ten seconds. Connection setup has its own timeout; these are not total
wall-time or I/O budgets. Accept a sample only after a zero exit and a complete
JSON result. A timeout, permission error, missing schema or partial result means
unknown, not a healthy zero; retain the previous good sample separately.

#### Catalog and file-size inventory

`table_bytes` includes TOAST and auxiliary table storage; `index_bytes` measures
indexes. `total_bytes` combines both. These physical observations are separate
function calls, so concurrent changes can make the components differ; read-only
MVCC does not freeze files or statistics. Database bytes already include these
relations: do not add database and relation totals together. Neither is free space.

Row/dead-tuple statistics are estimates, not exact counts or reclaimable bytes.
Use the analyze timestamps and modification count for context; do not run ANALYZE
or VACUUM as a side effect of sampling. Record collection time and deployment/
volume identity, since database names and OIDs alone do not distinguish clones or
restores. Measure local cost before choosing a polling frequency.

```sql
-- Catalog/file-size sample; no application-row count or modification.
BEGIN READ ONLY;
SET LOCAL statement_timeout = '5s';
SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '1s';
SET LOCAL timezone = 'UTC';
SET LOCAL search_path = pg_catalog;
WITH relations(oid) AS (
    VALUES
        ('public.container_creation_intents'::regclass),
        ('public.container_materializations'::regclass),
        ('public.container_cleanup_receipts'::regclass),
        ('public.runtime_capacity_holds'::regclass),
        ('public.outbox_events'::regclass),
        ('public.container_intent_redrives'::regclass),
        ('public.container_cleanup_redrives'::regclass)
), sizes AS (
    SELECT c.relname AS relation,
           c.oid,
           pg_table_size(c.oid) AS table_bytes,
           pg_indexes_size(c.oid) AS index_bytes,
           pg_total_relation_size(c.oid) AS total_bytes,
           s.n_live_tup AS estimated_live_rows,
           s.n_dead_tup AS estimated_dead_rows,
           s.n_mod_since_analyze,
           s.last_analyze,
           s.last_autoanalyze
    FROM relations r
    JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = r.oid
    LEFT JOIN pg_stat_user_tables s ON s.relid = c.oid
)
SELECT jsonb_build_object(
    'sampled_at', clock_timestamp(),
    'database', current_database(),
    'database_oid', (SELECT oid FROM pg_database WHERE datname = current_database()),
    'database_bytes', pg_database_size(current_database()),
    'server_version', current_setting('server_version'),
    'postmaster_started_at', pg_postmaster_start_time(),
    'read_only', current_setting('transaction_read_only'),
    'relations', (SELECT jsonb_agg(to_jsonb(s) ORDER BY relation) FROM sizes s)
);
COMMIT;
```

#### Exact retained-backlog diagnostic

This report scans application data; run it for diagnosis or a planned capacity
review, not on every worker/relay poll. Exact scans can consume CPU, I/O and temp
space and retain an MVCC snapshot. A timeout is a reason to inspect cost, not to
silently remove the deadline. Inventory and backlog are separate samples.

`MATCHED` means an existing receipt satisfies the pruning predicate's job,
container, runtime and intent comparison. Exact proof is checked first; only
unmatched rows are classified `INVALID_IDENTITY` or `MISSING`. Opaque container/
runtime strings remain untrimmed. Intent text follows pruning's canonical text
comparison: a valid but noncanonical payload UUID can be `MISSING`. This does not
normalize it into removal authority or validate a new RPC request.

Counts cover retained cleanup-action outbox rows, not lifetime cleanup or every
remaining intent/name obligation. Pruned transport disappears while proof and
name surveillance remain. A zero cleanup count does not establish that all work
or late-creation risk is gone. Active holds can represent live execution, not a
leak, and must not be added again to `runtime_nodes.running_jobs`. Marker/proof
mismatches call for diagnosis, never fabricated receipts or deletion. Whole-table
bytes cannot be assigned to individual cohorts using these counts.

```sql
-- On-demand full scans; timeout/error means unknown, never a healthy zero.
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ READ ONLY;
SET LOCAL statement_timeout = '10s';
SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '1s';
SET LOCAL timezone = 'UTC';
SET LOCAL search_path = pg_catalog, public;
WITH cleanup AS MATERIALIZED (
    SELECT e.topic,
           e.status::text AS publication_state,
           e.cleanup_state,
           CASE
               WHEN COALESCE((
                   SELECT r.intent_id::text = e.payload->'ContainerCleanup'->>'IntentID'
                   FROM public.container_cleanup_receipts r
                   WHERE r.job_id = CASE
                       WHEN pg_input_is_valid(e.payload->>'JobID', 'uuid')
                       THEN (e.payload->>'JobID')::uuid
                   END
                     AND r.container_id = e.payload->'ContainerCleanup'->>'ContainerID'
                     AND r.runtime_instance = e.payload->'ContainerCleanup'->>'RuntimeInstance'
               ), FALSE) THEN 'MATCHED'
               WHEN NOT COALESCE(pg_input_is_valid(e.payload->>'JobID', 'uuid'), FALSE)
                 OR NOT COALESCE(
                     pg_input_is_valid(e.payload->'ContainerCleanup'->>'IntentID', 'uuid'),
                     FALSE
                 )
                 OR COALESCE(e.payload->'ContainerCleanup'->>'ContainerID', '') = ''
                 OR COALESCE(e.payload->'ContainerCleanup'->>'RuntimeInstance', '') = ''
               THEN 'INVALID_IDENTITY'
               ELSE 'MISSING'
           END AS receipt,
           e.created_at
    FROM public.outbox_events e
    WHERE e.payload->>'Action' = 'CONTAINER_CLEANUP'
), groups AS (
    SELECT topic, publication_state, cleanup_state, receipt,
           count(*) AS rows,
           min(created_at) AS oldest_created_at
    FROM cleanup
    GROUP BY topic, publication_state, cleanup_state, receipt
)
SELECT jsonb_build_object(
    'sampled_at', statement_timestamp(),
    'database', current_database(),
    'read_only', current_setting('transaction_read_only'),
    'cleanup_groups', COALESCE((SELECT jsonb_agg(to_jsonb(g)
        ORDER BY topic, publication_state, cleanup_state, receipt) FROM groups g), '[]'::jsonb),
    'cleanup_rows', (SELECT count(*) FROM cleanup),
    'cleanup_without_exact_receipt', (
        SELECT count(*) FROM cleanup WHERE receipt <> 'MATCHED'
    ),
    'completed_without_exact_receipt', (
        SELECT count(*) FROM cleanup
        WHERE cleanup_state = 'COMPLETED' AND receipt <> 'MATCHED'
    ),
    'matched_receipt_without_completed_marker', (
        SELECT count(*) FROM cleanup
        WHERE receipt = 'MATCHED' AND cleanup_state IS DISTINCT FROM 'COMPLETED'
    ),
    'holds', (
        SELECT jsonb_build_object(
            'active', count(*) FILTER (WHERE released_at IS NULL),
            'released', count(*) FILTER (WHERE released_at IS NOT NULL)
        )
        FROM public.runtime_capacity_holds
    ),
    'ordinary_outbox_rows', (
        SELECT count(*) FROM public.outbox_events
        WHERE payload->>'Action' IS DISTINCT FROM 'CONTAINER_CLEANUP'
    ),
    'non_cleanup_rows_with_cleanup_state', (SELECT count(*) FROM public.outbox_events
        WHERE payload->>'Action' IS DISTINCT FROM 'CONTAINER_CLEANUP' AND cleanup_state IS NOT NULL)
);
COMMIT;
```

#### Capacity runway

Use existing filesystem, PVC or provider-quota monitoring for available/used
bytes, timestamps and storage-budget identity. Database size excludes WAL, logs,
backups and other databases/shared consumers. Map tables, indexes, TOAST and WAL
to their actual volumes using deployment/tablespace configuration; these reports
do not discover that mapping. Calculate each relevant volume separately.

For comparable samples over a representative interval:

```text
growth_bytes_per_day = (used_later - used_earlier) / elapsed_days
usable_headroom = max(0, available_now - operator_safety_reserve)
runway_days = usable_headroom / growth_bytes_per_day
```

Only calculate runway for positive representative growth. Missing history,
zero/negative growth, mismatched volumes, restores or resizes do not give a reliable
exhaustion forecast. Available bytes already exclude current usage; do not subtract
database size again. For illustration, 120 GiB available minus a 20 GiB reserve,
at a measured 5 GiB/day, gives 20 days. These are not defaults or a measurement of
your deployment. Choose reserve, review cadence and capacity alerts for the time
needed to expand storage. No storage threshold authorizes proof garbage collection.

See PostgreSQL's [size-function definitions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/functions-admin.html#FUNCTIONS-ADMIN-DBSIZE)
and [statistics semantics](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/monitoring-stats.html).

## Safe sequence

Measure backlog and latency, increase the constraining partition or store capacity, adjust worker replicas and concurrency, then confirm lease and retry behavior under failure.
</doc>

<doc title="Retries and recovery" path="./docs/operations/recovery/">
# Retries and recovery

## Outbox publication

Failed Kafka publication is retried with backoff under a processing lease. Exhausted rows become dead and remain visible for operational handling.

## Kafka handlers

Partition processing distinguishes retryable from terminal outcomes. Records are committed only when policy permits.

## Job execution

System failures can release eligible jobs for bounded retry. User workload failures are recorded without treating every failure as infrastructure instability.

## Expired leases

Recovery scans for expired running jobs, invalidates old ownership, attempts container cleanup, and either retries or terminates the job according to current state and retry limits.

## Stale events

Generation, dispatch attempt, deterministic ID, and lease-token checks intentionally reject delayed work. A precondition failure can therefore indicate successful protection rather than a platform outage.

## Container cleanup

Container cleanup is durable work with an immutable job, full container ID,
original runtime instance and creation-intent identity. It survives deletion of
its source job, workflow or owner. A worker stops the container, replays retained
logs when enabled, removes it, then records an exact-identity completion receipt.
A replay failure retains the container for another attempt.

Each cleanup generation permits three failed or abandoned attempts. An execution
lease lasts four minutes around the three-minute cleanup budget. Failures back off
for 30 seconds, then 60 seconds. Successfully reported caller cancellation refunds
its attempt; repeated interruptions can postpone cleanup indefinitely. After
exhaustion, persisted `QUARANTINED` lets the Kafka handler acknowledge that delivery
while retaining the unfinished obligation. Publication `DEAD` is a separate state requiring operator repair.

Successful cleanup publication schedules replay after five minutes by default;
successive successful waves wait ten, twenty, forty, then sixty minutes repeatedly.
`OUTBOX_RELAY_REPLAY_INTERVAL` and `OUTBOX_RELAY_REPLAY_MAX_INTERVAL` configure
these defaults with whole-millisecond precision. Durable pacing survives relay
restarts, and publication capacity is shared fairly with initial deliveries.
Consumer lag is not required. The cap is a scheduling interval, not a guaranteed
delivery deadline during overload, key blocking, lease/backoff delays or outages.
Ambiguous broker sends may still duplicate before that interval.

[Replay scheduling and ordering](./docs/engineering/transactional-outbox#claiming)

For grouped receipt/backlog counts and storage/runway interpretation, use the
[retained cleanup reports](./docs/operations/scaling#retained-cleanup-data).
These counts describe retained transport rows, not lifetime cleanup obligations.

### Administrative redrive

Repair the original runtime or configuration first. Call the internal jobs-service
`RedriveContainerCleanup` RPC over the deployment's authenticated TLS connection,
using an admin JWT for the jobs-service audience. The request contains:

```json
{
  "job_id": "<job UUID>",
  "container_id": "<full container ID>",
  "runtime_instance": "<original daemon ID>",
  "intent_id": "<creation intent UUID>",
  "generation": "1",
  "reason": "original daemon connectivity restored"
}
```

The generation is the observed **cleanup generation**, not workflow generation.
The repair reason is required, cannot be whitespace-only and is limited to 2048
bytes. The audit actor is derived from the validated JWT subject, never from
request fields or caller metadata. A shared credential identifies its principal,
not the individual human using it.

An accepted redrive increments the generation, resets execution/publication budgets
and requeues the original snapshot with initial-wave pacing. It may override `READY`, `RETRY`, quarantined
or expired-lease work, but refuses a live execution lease. Repeating an old generation
returns `STALE` without another reset or audit entry. A completion receipt returns
`COMPLETED` without requeueing. Redrive cannot retarget the original runtime,
manufacture removal proof, or repair a `COMPLETED` row that lacks exact receipt
proof. Do not issue raw `cleanup_state` updates or insert receipts without confirmed
removal.

The generation change and audit insert commit together. History retains the
immutable identity, authenticated actor, reason, expected/new generation and database
timestamp, independently of source rows or later outbox pruning:

```sql
SELECT job_id, container_id, runtime_instance, intent_id,
       expected_generation, generation, actor, reason, created_at
FROM container_cleanup_redrives
ORDER BY created_at DESC, event_key, generation
LIMIT 100;
```

See the [gRPC contract](./docs/internal/grpc-services#container-cleanup-rpcs) for
attempt/receipt RPCs and [monitoring](./docs/operations/monitoring#container-cleanup-signals)
for alert interpretation. Discovery inspection has its own `RedriveContainerIntent`
operation and audit history; it does not reopen execution authority.

<SourceLink path="docs/operations.md">Complete cleanup inspection and grpcurl runbook</SourceLink>

## Cleanup loops

Ordinary published outbox rows and processed-event records are pruned in bounded
batches after retention. Published unfinished container cleanup remains retained
until matching removal evidence exists, including after quarantine. Cleanup audit
history and creation-name discovery tombstones have no automatic expiry policy.
Age alone does not prove physical absence or authorize releasing a gate or hold.

Published-outbox pruning uses two candidate-limited lanes: ordinary published
events and `COMPLETED` cleanup awaiting exact receipt proof. A durable turn,
committed before lane work, alternates the preferred lane across replicas and
restarts; empty or failed calls still advance it. Busy reservations skip the call
with a debug log, so aligned replica schedules can reduce achieved throughput. Each call selects at most
`OUTBOX_RELAY_CLEANUP_BATCH_SIZE` candidate identities. The preferred lane is offered
half rounded up; the other lane receives the batch size
minus already charged candidates, and the
preferred lane gets at most one final borrowed operation. A failed lane is not
reentered in that call. Lanes lock candidates before proof, delete by candidate
ID and commit independently, so a partial call can return confirmed deletions
with an error. Failed lanes report charged allowances and zero known committed
deletions; `selected_known` marks whether the selection count was observed. Retained proof requires exact job, container, original-runtime and
text-intent matching; invalid job UUIDs and mismatched proof fail closed.

A `COMPLETED` row without exact proof is corruption and remains outside automatic
deletion. It can block the cleanup lane while ordinary pruning continues. Find
expired candidates lacking proof, replacing the interval with the configured
`OUTBOX_RELAY_PUBLISHED_RETENTION`:

```sql
SELECT events.id, events.published_at, events.payload->>'JobID' AS job_id,
       events.payload->'ContainerCleanup'->>'ContainerID' AS container_id,
       events.payload->'ContainerCleanup'->>'RuntimeInstance' AS runtime_instance,
       events.payload->'ContainerCleanup'->>'IntentID' AS intent_id,
       events.cleanup_state, events.cleanup_generation
FROM outbox_events events
WHERE events.status = 'PUBLISHED'
  AND events.published_at < now() - interval '168h'
  AND events.payload->>'Action' = 'CONTAINER_CLEANUP'
  AND events.cleanup_state = 'COMPLETED'
  AND NOT EXISTS (
      SELECT 1
      FROM container_cleanup_receipts receipt
      WHERE receipt.job_id = CASE
              WHEN pg_input_is_valid(events.payload->>'JobID', 'uuid')
              THEN (events.payload->>'JobID')::uuid
            END
        AND receipt.container_id = events.payload->'ContainerCleanup'->>'ContainerID'
        AND receipt.runtime_instance = events.payload->'ContainerCleanup'->>'RuntimeInstance'
        AND receipt.intent_id::text = events.payload->'ContainerCleanup'->>'IntentID'
  )
ORDER BY events.published_at, events.id
LIMIT 100;
```

Receipt-present rows whose cleanup state is not `COMPLETED`, including `NULL`,
are also outside pruning and indicate an invariant violation. Inspect them with:

```sql
SELECT events.id, events.status, events.published_at, events.cleanup_state,
       events.payload->>'JobID' AS job_id,
       events.payload->'ContainerCleanup'->>'ContainerID' AS container_id,
       events.payload->'ContainerCleanup'->>'RuntimeInstance' AS runtime_instance,
       events.payload->'ContainerCleanup'->>'IntentID' AS intent_id
FROM outbox_events events
JOIN container_cleanup_receipts receipt
  ON receipt.job_id = CASE
         WHEN pg_input_is_valid(events.payload->>'JobID', 'uuid')
         THEN (events.payload->>'JobID')::uuid
       END
 AND receipt.container_id = events.payload->'ContainerCleanup'->>'ContainerID'
 AND receipt.runtime_instance = events.payload->'ContainerCleanup'->>'RuntimeInstance'
 AND receipt.intent_id::text = events.payload->'ContainerCleanup'->>'IntentID'
WHERE events.payload->>'Action' = 'CONTAINER_CLEANUP'
  AND events.cleanup_state IS DISTINCT FROM 'COMPLETED'
ORDER BY events.published_at, events.id
LIMIT 100;
```

Audited administrative redrive is the repair path for unfinished cleanup under
its normal preconditions, not a way to mark corrupt rows complete or supply
missing proof.
</doc>

<doc title="Troubleshooting" path="./docs/operations/troubleshooting/">
# Troubleshooting

## TLS or certificate failures

Confirm `init-certs` completed and the failing service mounts the expected CA, certificate, and key. For a disposable local reset, use `down -v` and restart.

## Compose readiness

Find the first unhealthy dependency, not only the final service that failed to start. Check Kafka topic initialization and database migration output before worker logs.

## Missing logs

Confirm the workflow is `CONTAINER`, retention is enabled, the job logs processor is healthy, and ClickHouse plus Meilisearch are available. Heartbeat workflows and disabled retention intentionally have no retained logs.

## SSE does not stream

Confirm the job is running and use the production `/api/.../events` proxy path. Verify Nginx buffering is disabled and inspect `event: error` frames.

## Duplicate or stale events

Check idempotency-key reuse, outbox relay health, workflow generation mismatches, job lease ownership, and processor deduplication before treating a repeated Kafka record as corruption.

## Dashboard cannot reach the API

Verify `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL`, CORS origins, session cookie host and same-site policy, CSRF state, and the production Nginx path.

<SourceLink path="docs/operations.md">Expanded operational runbook</SourceLink>
</doc>

# Repository layout

| Path | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `cmd/` | Executable entry points for five domain services, the HTTP server, workers, processors, runtime agent, relay, and migrations |
| `internal/app/` | Interfaces between entry points and domain implementations; source for generated mocks |
| `internal/config/` | Typed environment-variable contracts for every Go process |
| `internal/model/` | Shared domain models and asynchronous event envelopes |
| `internal/server/` | Public HTTP gateway and middleware |
| `internal/service/` | Domain service logic |
| `internal/repository/` | Persistence and worker implementations; hosts the Testcontainers-backed integration tests as `*_integration_test.go` files |
| `internal/pkg/` | Shared infrastructure clients and reliability primitives; includes `testkit`, the shared Testcontainers bootstrap for repository integration tests, and the migration runners (`postgres.Migrate`, `clickhouse.Migrate`, `meilisearch.SetupIndexes`, `kafka.EnsureTopics`) |
| `proto/` | Source protobuf contracts |
| `pkg/proto/go/` | Generated Go protobuf code |
| `dashboard/` | Authenticated product dashboard |
| `static/` | Public landing page and static MDX documentation |
| `docs/` | Concise repository-level engineering references |
| `infra/k8s/` | Kustomize base plus local and production overlays; includes the operator runbook |
| `scripts/k8s/` | Kubernetes prerequisite, Secret bootstrap, render, validation, and apply workflow |
| `certs/` | Git-ignored local workspace populated and mounted by Compose certificate/bootstrap jobs |
| `compose.dev.yaml` | Locally built, debug-friendly full-stack topology |
| `compose.prod.yaml` | Published-image topology with Nginx, resource limits, and replicated workers |
| `Makefile` and `tools.go` | Generation, test, lint, build, run, and Kubernetes validation entry points |
| `.github/` | CI, release-image, and GitHub Pages deployment automation |

## Ownership pattern

Entry points compose configuration, infrastructure, repositories, and services. Business state transitions remain in domain layers; reusable transport and storage behavior belongs under `internal/pkg` only when it is truly cross-domain.

The dashboard follows the same ownership rule. Route files in `dashboard/src/app` are thin entry points, domain UI and hooks live together under `dashboard/src/features/<domain>`, reusable shadcn primitives remain under `dashboard/src/components/ui`, and only cross-feature API transport, endpoint construction, query keys, and general utilities belong under `dashboard/src/lib`.

Deployment ownership follows the same separation. `infra/k8s/base` owns shared application resources. `infra/k8s/overlays/local` and `infra/k8s/overlays/production` own strategy-specific infrastructure, storage, replica, and patch choices. `scripts/k8s/setup.sh` owns prerequisite and Secret bootstrap before Kustomize apply. Compose remains a separate supported topology rather than generated Kubernetes input.

## Generated files

Do not edit generated protobuf Go files by hand. Change the source files below `proto/` and run `make generate`; commit changes under `pkg/proto/go/` and `buf.lock` with the contract change.

Mocks below `internal/**/mock/` come from `//go:generate` directives. After changing an interface, run `make mockgen` and commit the resulting mock changes. Build artifacts under `.bin/`, `dashboard/.next/`, `static/.next/`, and `static/out/` are local output and are not source documentation.
</doc>

<doc title="Development workflow" path="./docs/contributing/development/">
# Development workflow

## Install tools and synchronize dependencies

```bash
make tools
make dependencies
```

`make tools` installs the repository's Go generators and linter into `.bin`; Buf itself must also be installed and available on `PATH`. `make dependencies` runs `make generate` and then `go mod tidy -v`. Generation removes and recreates `pkg/proto`, updates `buf.lock`, and compiles the protobuf contracts. Keep `proto/`, `pkg/proto/go/`, `buf.lock`, `go.mod`, and `go.sum` changes together when applicable.

Run the narrower target when only protobuf output needs verification:

```bash
make generate
```

After changing a Go interface with a `//go:generate` directive, regenerate mocks:

```bash
make mockgen
```

## Test

```bash
make test/short
make test/integration
```

`make test/short` runs every unit suite with the race detector; Docker-backed integration tests self-skip under `-short`. `make test/integration` selects every `TestIntegration*` test and needs a running Docker daemon: repository packages under `internal/repository`, the command ledger in `internal/pkg/commandidempotency` (both provisioned with Testcontainers), and the container workflow tests in `internal/pkg/kind/container` (which drive the host Docker daemon directly).

Integration package binaries use independent Testcontainers/Ryuk sessions through
a Python launcher. Local runs default to `INTEGRATION_PARALLELISM=1`; CI uses four
packages at a time. Set this value to match the Docker host's CPU and memory.
The launcher requires Python and preserves test arguments, exit codes and signals.
Race detection, fresh execution and every assertion remain enabled; tests are not
retried.

Integration tests live as `*_integration_test.go` files. Testcontainers-backed suites share a single bootstrap, `internal/pkg/testkit`, that starts one container per requested service in the package's `TestMain` (for example `testkit.Run(m, testkit.WithPostgres(), testkit.WithKafka())`), applies the embedded migrations and index setup, and terminates everything when the test binary finishes. The suite reuses the production clients and runners from the sibling `internal/pkg` packages: `postgres.Migrate`, `clickhouse.Migrate`, `meilisearch.SetupIndexes` and `kafka.EnsureTopics`. Tests therefore exercise the exact code paths services use without re-implementing migrations. Integration tests self-skip under `-short` or when Docker is unavailable (`testkit.RequireDocker` provides the same gate for direct-daemon suites), keeping `make test/short` fast on every machine.

## Lint and build

```bash
make lint
make build/all
cd dashboard && npm test && npm run lint && npm run build
cd ../static && npm run check
```

Use `npm ci` in both frontend workspaces when reproducing CI from their committed lockfiles. `npm run check` in `static/` validates the MDX/OpenAPI registry, lints, type-checks, and performs the static Next.js export.

Run Go lint as `./.bin/golangci-lint`, which is what `make lint` invokes. `make tools` installs a build of it there, and `GO_BIN` defaults to that directory. A `golangci-lint` found on `PATH` is usually a different build of a different Go toolchain; when it predates the Go version in `go.mod` it aborts with `can't load config: the Go language version ... is lower than the targeted Go version`, which reads like a config bug but is only a toolchain mismatch. To lint a subset, pass package patterns to the pinned binary: `./.bin/golangci-lint run ./internal/pkg/kafka/...`.

Dashboard route modules should remain thin. Keep domain components, hooks, and API response types under `dashboard/src/features/<domain>`; reserve `dashboard/src/components/ui` for reusable shadcn primitives and `dashboard/src/lib` for infrastructure shared by multiple features.

## Dependency updates

Keep Go modules and tools, both npm lockfiles, Docker base images, Compose and
Kubernetes service images, integration-test fixtures, and CI toolchains aligned.
Use stable versions supported by their plugins and framework dependencies;
updating only a direct package can leave an unsupported toolchain. Regenerate
protobuf output and run the existing checks after changing its generators.

Review certificate verification in the runtime and operating system as well as
SDK dependencies. Rebuild images to pick up refreshed CA packages and restart
processes to activate them. See [Certificates and security](./docs/deployment/security)
for the Node trust-store policy.

## Kubernetes changes

Render and client-dry-run both overlays after changing `infra/k8s`, `scripts/k8s`, deployment configuration, image arguments, ports, probes, or Secrets:

```bash
make k8s/render/local
make k8s/render/production
make k8s/dry-run/local
make k8s/dry-run/production
scripts/k8s/setup.sh --mode local --dry-run
scripts/k8s/setup.sh --mode production --context <context> --dry-run
```

The render targets work offline. The kubectl client dry runs still use API discovery and therefore need a reachable selected cluster; full OpenAPI schema validation likewise needs a live target cluster or a separate validator such as `kubeconform`. The setup-script dry runs additionally exercise prerequisite, existing-Secret inspection, and Secret preparation logic against the selected kubectl context.

## Documentation changes

Add or edit MDX under `static/content/docs`, update `static/docs.config.ts`, and update `static/content/openapi.yaml` when the public HTTP contract changes. Run `npm run generate:llms` after changing any of those canonical sources; `npm run validate:llms` rejects stale `llms.txt` or `llms-full.txt` artifacts, and the static build runs this drift check automatically. Keep the concise repository references under `docs/`, `README.md`, `infra/k8s/README.md`, and landing-page copy aligned when the same behavior is described there. From `static/`, `npm run validate:docs` rejects unregistered pages, duplicate slugs, missing source references, broken docs links, and invalid OpenAPI.

Operational SQL and prose mirrored between `docs/operations.md` and the matching
MDX page must be updated together. Explicitly compare both copies: `validate:docs`
checks the static documentation, and `validate:llms` checks generated artifacts,
but neither compares the standalone operations guide with MDX. Revalidate the
published SQL when its executable statements change.

## Releases

Git tags matching `v*` trigger service image release jobs after lint, build, generated-protobuf verification, and tests complete. The static site validates and deploys from `main` through GitHub Pages.
</doc>
